sections.title: Review and lock one variant at a time
sections.body: Name the shape and closer, show the complete email and wait for feedback. Save corrections. The source library aims for ten to fifteen approved step-one variants, with exactly two cold sequence steps. A small review can start with one variant; do not invent variety just to meet a quota.

sections.title: Keep meaning fixed when formatting
sections.body: Subject is canonical first_name, mapped to the tool. Email two is one line in the original thread. Add spintax only after wording is locked and the tool syntax is verified. No unsupported results, borrowed names or unapproved signal references. Render before loading.

prompt: Run cold-email-copy on approved offer.md, profile, proof and research. Draft variant 1 only, name its shape and closer and show five rendered examples. Wait for feedback. Lock only after approval. Keep exactly two cold steps and do not upload or send.
actions: Judge the message as the actual buyer.
Verify claims and the thing offered in the reply ask.
Approve the final version and keep later changes reviewable.
example: The example copy offers to show a target list and opportunity definition. It makes no invented case-study claim.
failure: If the offer itself is unclear, return to the offer file. More copy variants will not fix an undefined service.

title: Check sender health and useful campaign signals
description: Detect problems without guessing what the reports mean.
finish: A health report with checked, listed and unknown results.
needs: Exact sender inventory, tool access, dated results and approved review settings.

sections.title: Use several kinds of evidence
sections.body: Check connection/authentication, bounces, sends, human replies and per-domain trends. Source warm-up and reply-rate thresholds are review heuristics, not universal guarantees. Investigate before changing infrastructure or blaming the offer.

sections.title: Treat DNS limitations honestly
sections.body: A blocklist can refuse your resolver. Mark that UNKNOWN, not clean. Confirm the IP you test is an actual outbound sending IP; an MX IP may only receive mail. Keep domain listings separate from IP listings. The full supplied skill explains technical handling.

sections.title: Recommend a response, do not silently change the account
sections.body: A listed sender, bounce spike or sudden loss of replies should produce a specific recommendation with evidence. Pausing, rotating, retiring or changing volume needs approval. Do not use open-rate reporting as the main decision measure when tracking is disabled.

prompt: Run sending-domain-blacklist and weekly-campaign-report for the approved sender group. Record source/time, complete inventory, domain/IP distinction, unknown checks and trends. Recommend action with evidence. Do not change DNS, pause mailboxes, raise limits or send tests.
actions: Check the exact sender group and reporting period.
Resolve unknown mandatory checks before a later load.
Approve infrastructure changes separately.
example: A refused lookup says UNKNOWN and blocks a claim that all checks are clean.
failure: If the connector fails, report it. Do not reuse last week's result as if it were current.

title: Optional: use LinkedIn by hand
description: Follow up on relevant people without automated account activity.
finish: A manual prospect-review and message-draft process.
needs: Approved offer, relevant person, permitted public information and owner-selected activity window.

sections.title: Keep this outside the required launch
sections.body: The core path is email. LinkedIn can support relevant follow-up or account research after that path works. Do not buy another tool or delay launch just because an optional channel exists.

sections.title: Use AI off-platform
sections.body: Research and draft where permitted, then review and act manually. The supplied L1 and skills pack disagree on 30 versus 60 days for activity screening. Choose a written window for the actual campaign; do not disguise it as a proven rule.

sections.title: Keep the same offer and context
sections.body: An email lead moved to LinkedIn should not receive a contradictory pitch. Track prior contact and opt-outs. Reaching another person at the same account requires its own relevance and approval. Do not automate clicks, invites or messages from this preview.

prompt: Prepare an optional LinkedIn research and draft checklist using approved profile, offer and exclusions. Flag the unresolved activity window and role rules. No platform login, scraping, connection request, posting or sending. Return drafts only.
actions: Choose the activity window and relevant roles.
Review every proposed message in context.
Perform any later platform action manually within the account's rules.
example: A draft can refer to an approved prior interaction without inventing familiarity.
failure: If access or policy is unclear, keep the step manual and optional. Never bypass a platform block.

title: Optional: distinguish a warm caller from a backstop
description: Give each calling role a clear purpose and budget.
finish: A role brief and escalation rule.
needs: Actual service scope, approved phone-contact policy, quotes and clear ownership.

sections.title: Warm caller or SDR
sections.body: This person follows up interested email leads and helps convert real interest into booked meetings. The source describes an ongoing role, often base pay plus a booking fee. It is not a replacement for processing replies correctly.

sections.title: Delivery backstop caller
sections.body: This is separately budgeted support if a channel underperforms against an agreed engagement. Obtain real quotes and a deliverable definition before including it. A caller does not make success universal or remove your delivery risk.

sections.title: Write the handoff
sections.body: Give the caller the original offer, thread context, fit rules, permitted claims, contact rules and booking process. Keep opt-outs, exact identity and results visible. This preview does not call anyone or place a person.

prompt: Draft separate warm-SDR and delivery-backstop role briefs from the approved scope. Include tasks, input, permitted claims, booking definition, reporting and budget assumptions. Do not recruit, contact leads or promise a hire.
actions: Confirm the role needed.
Use actual quotes and costs.
Review phone-contact rules and scripts before any live use.
example: A warm caller handles a known interested lead; a backstop is a separate costed delivery route.
failure: Do not treat a generic caller promise as proof that the engagement can be delivered.

title: Cold-email terms in plain words
description: Keep the measurements and workflow stages distinct.
finish: Definitions you can use when reading a report or asking for help.
needs: No prerequisite. Return to the glossary when a term is unfamiliar.

sections.title: People and files
sections.body: ICP: the type of company and person you want to reach. Lead: a person/company record. Qualified: passes the written rules. Raw list: untouched export. Held: cannot proceed until reviewed. Suppression: a person/domain excluded from contact. SEG: a security filter in front of a recipient's mailbox.

sections.title: Campaign and reply
sections.body: Sequencer: tool that sends the approved email sequence. Variant: a different approved version of a step. Bump: follow-up in the same thread. Interested: a reply showing relevant interest, not every human reply. Booking: calendar event. Opportunity: the commercial milestone defined with the client.

sections.title: Numbers and evidence
sections.body: LTV: customer revenue over their whole relationship, unless a different definition is explicitly stated. ACV: annual contract value. Gross profit: revenue minus direct delivery costs. Cash collected: money actually received. Lead runway: eligible new contacts remaining divided by daily NEW contacts. UNKNOWN: the data was not available or verified.

prompt: Explain an unfamiliar report using these definitions. Identify the metric, source, denominator and period. Do not replace an unavailable metric with a different one or infer profit from revenue.
actions: Ask which metric is actually meant.
Check the period and denominator.
Return to the relevant operating step.
example: Twenty sends may include ten first emails and ten bumps, so daily sends and new contacts are not interchangeable.
failure: If a report uses a term differently, name the difference before comparing results.

title: Use the two-call sales process
description: Discover the business first, then review a specific scope.
finish: A sales path with a purpose and output for each stage.
needs: A relevant prospect, approved offer, price range and discovery preparation.

sections.title: Call one: understand and define
sections.body: Prepare from the actual business, then let the prospect explain their goals and process. Walk from first interest to sale. Confirm value, sales cycle, capacity, decision-makers and the milestone they consider a real opportunity. Do not give a long technical tour or ask questions you could have researched.

sections.title: Between calls: write a forwardable scope
sections.body: Send continuity on the same thread, then a short proposal reflecting their words. Give one clear feedback request and the review date. The internal champion should be able to forward it without retelling your pitch.

sections.title: Call two: decide on the actual deal
sections.body: Restate the goal and agreed scope, ask which concerns remain, work through the opportunity definition and terms and identify the decision. Agree a next step and owner. Do not pretend every buyer needs identical pressure or a scripted close. [Use discovery](/resources/resources/sales/discovery), [between-call emails](/resources/resources/sales/between-calls), [proposal](/resources/resources/sales/proposal) and [objection examples](/resources/resources/sales/objections).

prompt: Build a two-call plan from the approved offer and prospect notes. Specify the goal, questions, output and next action for discovery, between-call work and review. Use only agreed numbers. Prepare drafts, not sends.
actions: Complete preparation and discovery notes.
Confirm proposal review with the right people.
Record what was agreed before agreement/payment.
example: The proposal review begins with the buyer's actual questions because they received a clear scope beforehand.
failure: If call one did not establish the business process, do not fill the proposal with assumptions. Ask for the missing facts.

title: Run discovery with the supplied script
description: Find the commercial gap and the client's definition of value.
finish: Completed discovery notes that can produce a real proposal.
needs: Website preparation, approved range, service boundaries and permission for any recording.

sections.title: Open briefly and let them speak
sections.body: Acknowledge one researched fact, ask what they are focused on and what they want over the next 90 days. The point is to understand their business, not perform expertise you do not have.

sections.title: Walk the process instead of skipping to price
sections.body: Ask what happens after initial interest, who speaks with the buyer, what makes it worth pursuing, when a proposal/pilot happens, how many convert and how long that takes. Write the sequence in their words. Confirm capacity and decision-makers.

sections.title: Close with approach, range and review
sections.body: Explain the proposed route in a few sentences. State the real range and payment shape you are considering. Arrange a review with relevant people and say when the scope will arrive. The downloadable script contains the full question bank and notes fields.

prompt: Read the discovery script and prospect's public facts. Prepare five to seven relevant questions, a process map and the known range. After the call extract exact statements, numbers and concerns with transcript references. Mark missing facts. Do not invent answers or send a proposal.
actions: Practise the opening, then use the process questions naturally.
Record exact values with their period, not just a dollar amount.
Approve the completed notes before drafting the proposal.
example: First interest → needs discussion → site review → scoped quotation could be a maintenance buyer's path. Confirm it, do not assume it.
failure: If you do not understand an industry term, ask the buyer. Do not hide the uncertainty behind an AI summary.

title: Use the five between-call emails
description: Keep a proposal moving with one clear request.
finish: A continuity email, proposal email and appropriate follow-up drafts.
needs: Completed discovery notes, real review date and a draft proposal.

sections.title: Keep the context together
sections.body: Use the same sales thread from continuity through revisions, agreement and invoice. The source recommends prompt continuity after discovery and a proposal within a day or two. Those are preparation targets, not permission to send.

sections.title: Ask for one useful thing
sections.body: Name the person, requested review, location, date and what it unlocks. “Looks good” is weaker than specific confirmation or a concern. Ask what decision-makers will question first and answer it in writing.

sections.title: Use the template that matches the stage
sections.body: The file contains continuity, proposal delivery, pre-review, terms-agreed and stalled-decision templates. Replace every placeholder and verify dates, attachment, links and actual agreement. A changed price or recipient needs another review.

prompt: Use discovery notes, proposal and the five between-call templates to draft only the email appropriate to the current stage. One ask, one owner, one date. Keep actual terms and thread identity. Show missing facts and do not send.
actions: Choose the current sales stage.
Review exact copy, recipients, links and dates.
Approve any future send separately.
example: After discovery, the buyer receives a scoped question to answer before the review, not a random sequence of generic follow-ups.
failure: If the prospect changed the scope, update the proposal first. Do not keep sending an old automated sequence.

title: Build the proposal from discovery
description: Show understanding, work handled and agreed terms.
finish: A concise proposal and a forwardable decision-maker note.
needs: Approved discovery notes, scope, price range, proof and responsibilities.

sections.title: Lead with the buyer's situation
sections.body: Write a two-to-three-sentence abstract: what you discussed, what they want and what you propose. Use their actual language. A partner who missed the call should understand the basic deal from this.

sections.title: Explain how the work gets done
sections.body: Show targeting, sources, lists, messaging, qualification and ongoing work where included. Give an honest market estimate and conservative conversion reasoning only when sourced. Describe the opportunity definition, what the client must do and what you cannot control.

sections.title: Make the commercial decision clear
sections.body: State budget, payment trigger, term, minimum and remedy as agreed. Close with review, start process and a short note for other decision-makers. The editable template contains every section and the extraction instruction. Final agreement follows accepted terms.

prompt: Read discovery notes and approved offer/proof. Extract exact goals, process, numbers, concerns, decision-makers and quoted range with references. Draft proposal.md in its supplied structure. Mark anything not agreed. Never invent fees, case studies, market sizes or conversion rates. Do not send.
actions: Check the draft against the actual call.
Resolve every missing commercial fact.
Review the abstract and decision-maker note as someone who missed the call.
example: The maintenance proposal explains what an accepted pursuit means and when the second payment is earned, rather than hiding behind a long deck.
failure: If the AI cannot trace a number to the call or approved standard term, remove it or mark it pending.

title: Use the right asset at the right sales stage
description: Answer the buyer's next question without sending everything.
finish: A small asset set matched to discovery, review and kickoff.
needs: Approved offer, buyer concerns, proof and actual sales path.

sections.title: Before the call
sections.body: A pre-call page explains agenda, attendees, preparation and how to reschedule. A relevant sample or short VSL can help a buyer understand the service. Do not force every asset on every prospect.

sections.title: Between discovery and decision
sections.body: Use a short system overview, evidence matched to the concern, the actual proposal and a forwardable note. A lead magnet should solve a useful small job itself, not just advertise that you know the answer.

sections.title: After acceptance
sections.body: The agreement, invoice and kickoff information should agree on scope and responsibilities. The asset template gives a stage-by-stage checklist. External Canva/Notion assets from the old library remain preserved in source but are not labelled verified here.

prompt: Map the approved buyer questions to the minimum useful assets. Draft a pre-call page, system overview and decision-maker note using the supplied file. Show source-backed proof and missing assets. Do not invent testimonials or publish.
actions: Ask what the buyer needs to decide next.
Send only a reviewed, appropriate asset after separate approval.
Verify actual access before sharing a link.
example: A proposal addresses their scope; a process deck explains how the work happens. They do different jobs.
failure: If an external template is unavailable, use the local outline and report the access gap instead of promising a download that does not exist.

title: Handle objections by finding the real concern
description: Use example dialogue and a decision process, not reflexive discounts.
finish: A practice response for the buyer's actual concern.
needs: The accepted scope, real value/cost evidence and authority over any proposed terms.

sections.title: Clarify before answering
sections.body: Ask which part makes the buyer uncertain: value, ability to deliver, timing, budget, cash flow or internal approval. Restate it and check you understood. A concern about delivery is not fixed by splitting the payment.

sections.title: Practice example: price and terms
sections.body:
Example dialogue demonstrating the source method, not a verbatim sales-call transcript:

Buyer: “That is more than we planned.”

Agency: “Is the concern the total budget, or paying it before you see the work?”

Buyer: “Mostly the upfront part.”

Agency: “If the scope makes sense, we can look at a payment split tied to the agreed work. Which timing would fit your budget?”

Any revised split must still fund delivery and be approved. Do not automatically discount or invent a guarantee.

sections.title: Practice example: could do it internally
sections.body:
Buyer: “We could buy these tools ourselves.”

Agency: “You could. The engagement covers the buyer research, list checks, copy testing, reply work and reporting we agreed to run. Which part would your team want to own, and what would that take away from?”

Use only tasks you actually perform. Explain the real trade-off in work and coordination, not secret access or assumed incompetence.

sections.title: Get a clear next action
sections.body: Source T5 offers possible changes to amount, split, fee credit, minimum and remedy. These are options requiring commercial judgement, not an automatic ladder to concede everything. If the buyer is unsuitable or the terms do not work, decline respectfully.

prompt: Using the actual objection, discovery notes and approved terms, identify the likely concern and draft one clarifying question and a grounded response. Separate value concerns from payment timing. Do not invent proof, discount, guarantee or change terms. Label practice dialogue as an example, not an actual transcript.
actions: Name the concern in the buyer's words.
Check whether your response actually addresses it.
Review and approve any commercial change.
example: A payment split can address timing after the buyer accepts the value. It does not establish value by itself.
failure: If the promise cannot be delivered or believed from the evidence, fix that issue rather than pressuring the buyer.

title: Explain what all the work adds up to
description: Make the useful business change visible without inventing bonuses.
finish: A clear explanation of outcome, mechanism and responsibility.
needs: Approved scope and buyer problem, not a wish list.

sections.title: Connect each component to a job
sections.body: Research chooses a relevant buyer; qualification removes poor fits; copy creates useful interest; reply handling turns interest into a next step; reporting shows what to fix. Describe the finished work and what the buyer no longer has to coordinate.

sections.title: Keep the desired state credible
sections.body: More valuable deals can create margin for delivery help. Standard scope and processes can reduce owner dependence. These are causal possibilities with conditions, not universal measured results.

sections.title: Upsell only a useful next job
sections.body: Offer additional work when the current result creates a real need and you can deliver it. State extra scope, owner, price and timing separately. Do not disguise necessary core delivery as a surprise add-on.

prompt: Turn the approved scope into a plain explanation of business value, actual provider work, output, buyer job and limitations. Do not add services, bonuses, invented cost comparisons or historical results.
actions: Check each component exists in the scope.
Explain its commercial use.
Separate optional additional work from the core engagement.
example: A maintained reply process is valuable because relevant replies are reviewed and progressed, not because its name contains AI.
failure: If an outcome relies on the buyer's closing or service quality, name that dependency.

title: Keep long-term nurture separate from booking follow-ups
description: Respect timing, intent and the original offer.
finish: A dated review plan for leads who are not ready now.
needs: Full thread, permission/contact status, actual request and campaign context.

sections.title: Use the reply workflow first
sections.body: Interested replies, questions, referrals, opt-outs and bookings belong in the daily reply process. Short follow-ups after offering times are part of booking. Do not enrol the same person in a separate nurture path without checking the current thread and permissions.

sections.title: Record a specific future reason
sections.body: If someone says later, record when and why. A dated reminder is different from a new automated sequence. Send only useful, relevant material aligned with what they asked about and the original service.

sections.title: Stop when the situation changes
sections.body: A reply, booking, opt-out or changed offer cancels inappropriate scheduled follow-up. Check the latest state before any future message. This preview drafts reminders only; it does not create live workflows.

prompt: Review the full lead thread and campaign context. Distinguish active booking follow-up from a later nurture request. Draft a dated plan with reason, useful asset and approval boundary. Do not enrol, schedule or send.
actions: Confirm the actual requested timing.
Check contact status before a future send.
Keep the follow-up queue and nurture plan from overlapping.
example: A lead asking to revisit next quarter should not keep getting this week's proposed meeting slots.
failure: If permission or intent is unclear, hold the action and ask the owner.

title: Onboard a client with the complete form and kickoff
description: Collect the facts your agents and operator actually need.
finish: An approved profile, offer, proof, fit rules and settings for the client.
needs: The accepted service scope, authorised client contact and secure access process.

sections.title: Collect useful detail once
sections.body: The downloadable form preserves the existing 23-question structure: business, target market, technologies, ideal clients, exclusions, keywords, service, buyer questions, pains, proof, guarantee, useful assets, differentiation, current/target meetings, capacity and success definition.

sections.title: Add the system inputs
sections.body: Confirm customer value and period, actual sales cycle, opportunity milestone, calendar owner/event/duration/time zone, sender identity, spend caps and approval owner. Passwords and API keys do not belong in the form.

sections.title: Use kickoff to resolve gaps
sections.body: Walk through answers, delivery boundaries and acceptance. Agree research, list and copy review points. Create the five client files from the form with source references. Unknowns remain visible. End with owner, deliverable and next date, not a vague promise to start.

prompt: Use onboarding.md and client-profile-instruction.md to extract the five working files from the client's actual answers and approved scope. Cite the supplied answer for each fact. Flag missing capacity, economics, permissions or responsibility. Do not create accounts or campaigns.
actions: Review the completed form and key unknowns.
Confirm calendar, opportunity definition and scope at kickoff.
Approve the extracted files before research.
example: A completed form becomes usable agent inputs rather than a document nobody reads again.
failure: If the client response conflicts with what was sold, resolve the scope before launching.

title: Train or hire the person who supervises the work
description: Define the job before asking someone to run the system.
finish: A role brief, practical assessment and supervised handover plan.
needs: A documented process, clear work volume, real budget and a named manager.

sections.title: Choose the missing job
sections.body: An inbox operator checks fit/cards, approvals and bookings. A GTM operator may prepare lists, campaigns and reports. A CSM handles the agreed client communication and escalations. AI can perform parts of those jobs, but someone still owns quality and exceptions.

sections.title: Use a practical assessment
sections.body: Give each candidate the same synthetic reply/list task and score fit judgement, writing, evidence use, identity/time-zone accuracy and escalation. Do not let applicants contact prospects or use real credentials. The supplied role brief includes the questions and assessment.

sections.title: Onboard with supervision
sections.body: Start with narrow access and a known queue. Demonstrate, let them repeat, inspect errors and clarify when to escalate. Set working hours, cover, reporting and approval boundaries explicitly. The original wage and time-zone examples were illustrative and should not become current defaults. A recruiting resource does not mean CCS guarantees a placed employee.

prompt: Draft a scoped operator brief and fixture-only assessment using operator-brief.md. Map tasks to AI, operator, owner and CCS. Use actual hours and budget when supplied, otherwise flag them. Do not recruit, send messages, hire or grant access.
actions: Name the actual work and success standard.
Use the same practical rubric for candidates.
Supervise before expanding responsibility.
example: The operator can correctly hold a misfit reply and an unavailable slot without asking for every routine decision.
failure: If the job depends on undocumented owner knowledge, improve the process before calling the role ready.

title: Use SOPs and a weekly operating review
description: Reduce repeated decisions without hiding exceptions.
finish: One complete SOP and a weekly decision record.
needs: Current process, owner, inputs, outputs and real exceptions.

sections.title: Document a job someone can finish
sections.body: State result, trigger, owner, input files, access, steps, approvals, checks, failures and handoff. A video can help but should not hide changing settings or escalation rules. The local template includes a complete runway-review example.

sections.title: Review capacity, economics and quality separately
sections.body: More customers can raise revenue and still reduce profit or overwhelm delivery. Review actual fees, direct costs, capacity, client acceptance and owner time. Compare more work for current clients with more clients only after the delivery process is stable.

sections.title: Change one observed bottleneck
sections.body: Inspect campaign evidence, client feedback and operating errors. Assign a specific correction and next review date. Do not replace strategy repeatedly without diagnosing whether the issue is audience, message, sending, replies, sales or delivery.

prompt: Using actual workflow notes, draft one SOP with result, owner, trigger, files, steps, approval boundaries, checks and failure handling. Prepare a weekly operating review that separates revenue, profit, capacity and owner dependence. No live changes.
actions: Have another operator follow the SOP on a safe example.
Record the hidden steps they needed.
Correct it and agree who maintains it.
example: The completed SOP calculates runway from new contacts and names the next owner rather than automatically buying more leads.
failure: If the operator needs verbal rescue, the SOP is not complete. Add the missing decision or escalation.

title: All templates and the AI pack
description: Get the file you need, with its purpose and version.
finish: The exact versioned files used by Install, Resources and Training.
needs: Choose a lesson first if you do not know which file you need. This is an index of the same assets, not another course.

sections.title: Start with the full pack
sections.body: The ZIP contains shared agent rules, all 16 source-derived skills, working-file templates and the completed example. Install and Training refer to version 0.1.0-preview. The pack is for review and drafts, with external writes disabled. Downloading it does not install Grok skills or connect accounts.

sections.title: Use the blank templates for your own business
sections.body: Complete profile, offer, proof, fit rules and settings first. Research and campaign files come next. Discovery, between-call emails, proposal, onboarding, operator brief and SOPs support the relevant jobs. Read the file's completion check and keep unknown facts visible.

sections.title: Compare with the completed example
sections.body: The example uses consistent fictional company records on reserved .example domains, illustrative fees and a clearly marked local simulation. It is not a CCS member case study. The completed proposal traces facts to discovery exercise notes and leaves unagreed terms pending.

prompt: Inventory the supplied pack by manifest version. Explain which file is needed for my current step and which inputs I must supply. Do not start a new workflow, duplicate the whole course or assume the example is my business. No external actions.
actions: Use the asset linked from your current lesson.
